title: My Job: Naomi Coquillon
content:
Naomi Coquillon is chief of interpretation in the Center for Exhibits and Interpretation. She recently received a 2026 Librarian of Congress Award for her role in developing and opening The Source, the Library’s new youth center.

Tell us about your background.

I’ve been working in museums and libraries for 20 years. I have an undergraduate degree in history and literature, a master’s degree in history and a master’s degree in museum education. There’s really no better place for me to be than at the Library.

What brought you to the Library, and what do you do?

title: Teddy Roosevelt’s “Bullet” Speech
content:
-This story was written with Elaina Finkelstein, a public affairs specialist in the Office of Communications.

Teddy Roosevelt was a sturdy sort, and nothing as trifling as a wee bullet wound was going to stop him from giving a speech.

Roosevelt was shot in the chest on Oct. 14, 1912, while running for reelection to the White House. He was leaving the Hotel Gilpatrick in Milwaukee, on his way to the city’s auditorium for a campaign speech.  There was a crowd, and as he was about to step into his automobile, a mentally unstable man named John Schrank pulled out a .38 Colt revolver and shot him at close range.

The bullet, according to the Theodore Roosevelt Center, “passed through a folded copy of his lengthy address, his glasses case, and his heavy winter coat. The bullet broke his fourth rib and lodged near his right lung. Doctors determined that the bullet should not be removed.”

Roosevelt, 53 and famously adventurous, scarcely seemed to mind. He stopped the crowd from assaulting Schrank, then went to the auditorium and spoke — for more than an hour.

title: Genealogy in Colonial America: The Ties that Mattered
content:
-This is a guest post by A J  Aiséirithe, a reference librarian in the History and Genealogy Section of the Main Reading Room.

Genealogy was everywhere in Colonial America, affecting if not dictating marriage prospects, business contacts and the eligibility to inherit property.

Genealogy was so intertwined with the law — particularly about inheritance — that genealogy practically was the law in ways we don’t fully understand today, said Karin Wulf, a Brown University professor of history, at a recent Afternoons with the Library event.

“People think that genealogy is something they do about their individual families,” Wulf said, adding that it is often regarded as a hobby or curiosity. But in the Colonial era, she said, “… it was about intimacy, it was about emotion, it was about affection and it was about structures of power, economics and law. All of those things could be true at the same time.”

Wulf was on hand to discuss the research in her new book, “Lineage: Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America,”  which was carried out in part at the Library.

title: Death of the Magician: 100th Anniversary of Houdini’s Tragic Death
content:
Harry Houdini died 100 years ago this Halloween, the master magician shuffling off this mortal coil on Oct. 31, 1926, in a series of events that, like most of his sensational career, has always been seen in light and shadow, in plain sight but not entirely clear.

He bequeathed his astonishing library — one of the world’s largest private collections of books on magic, witchcraft, demonology, spiritualism and psychic phenomena, about 4,000 books in all, going back to 1489 – to the Library of Congress, so that it would be readily available to the public, which it is! Drop by anytime; it’s in the Rare Book and Special Collections Division. There are also personal scrapbooks and the like.

But his real final act — the Prestige, in the parlance — was that he died but never really disappeared.

A century on, he remains a one-word incantation of mystery, of things that can’t quite be explained, as if he had just walked out of a weird tale by his buddy H.P. Lovecraft, the legendary horror master.

title: Some of the Spookiest Specters in the Library’s Archives
content:
What’s the scariest part of working at a library? The ghost writers.  

Library staffers aren’t easily spooked — as proved by a recent presentation on some of the collection’s most haunting finds, just in time for Halloween. 

In the Prints and Photographs Division, spirit photography in the 19th century reflected how grief and loss fueled a spiritualism phase in the 1850s and 1860s, explained archivist Maggie McCready. The massive loss of life during the Civil War, combined with Victorian anxiety about death, led to a desire to connect with deceased loved ones.  

Enter photographers such as William H. Mumler, who claimed to show spirits in their images. The reality? Using old glass plate negatives left a ghostly image behind on the new photograph.  

Scandal struck when it turned out that one of the “spirits” in a Mumler photo was, in fact, alive. A few years later, in 1869, New York authorities ran a sting operation and arrested Mumler for fraud. The prosecution’s star witness was P. T. Barnum (not known for his adherence to the truth), who was photographed in a phony spirit image featuring Abraham Lincoln.
snippet: What’s the scariest part of working at a library? The ghost writers.
creator: Hannah Ostroff

title: Mary Lincoln: “A nice, chatty little letter” Shortly Before the Assassination of her Husband
content:
On Wednesday, Feb. 15, 1865, Mary Lincoln sat down before a lined sheet of paper, which was bordered in black, marking that she was still mourning the death of her son Willie three years earlier, the second of the Lincoln children to die of a childhood illness. In tight, perfect penmanship, she dashed off a short letter to her friend Caroline Wright.

She thanked Wright for sending along a wreath of hair, advised her that the Executive Mansion (as the White House was then called) was in the midst of remodeling and thus it would be best if Wright and her husband stayed at the nearby Willard Hotel for an upcoming visit.

“We will be deprived of several charming visitors, yourselves included, on the 1rst of March,” she wrote, referring to the period around her husband’s second inauguration. “Yet … we will be happy to have you dine with us and see you frequently.”

She wrote that she was interrupted just then, must close, and signed off with kind regards as “Mary Lincoln,” the way she always did after she married.

title: John J. Audubon’s Breathtaking Book of Birds
content:
—This is a guest post by Ashley Rose Young, a curator in the Rare Book and Special Collections Division. It also appears in the September/October issues of the Library of Congress Magazine.

In the early 19th century, John James Audubon set out to do something no natural history illustrator had attempted at such scale: depict North American birds at life size, in vivid, animated poses. The result was “The Birds of America,” one of the most ambitious — and physically imposing — sets of books ever produced.

Published between 1827 and 1838, the work was issued as a series of hand-colored engravings, printed on enormous “double elephant” sheets measuring roughly 38 by 26 inches. Audubon partnered with the London engraver Robert Havell Jr. to translate his paintings into prints of remarkable precision and color.

Subscribers received the plates in installments, eventually assembling a collection that included 435 illustrations depicting 489 species of birds. All that paper adds up: Typically bound in four volumes, “The Birds of America” can be astonishingly heavy. The Library’s set totals 196 pounds, with the largest volume weighing a whopping 55 pounds.

title: David Harrington, the Kronos Quartet and the American Folklife Center
content:
— This is a guest post by David Harrington, the founder and artistic director of San Francisco’s Grammy Award-winning Kronos Quartet. It also appears in the September/October issue of the Library of Congress Magazine. In 2024, the Library appointed Harrington the Kluge Chair in Modern Culture and announced its acquisition of the Kronos archives. The quartet’s 1992 album “Pieces of Africa” was inducted into the National Recording Registry.

Whenever a creative project of the Kronos Quartet reveals a need for information deeply embedded in the complex world of American traditional music, the first call I make is to the American Folklife Center. The AFC, through its expert, generous, helpful staff and rich archival holdings, has demonstrated again and again what a treasure we have available to us as patrons of the Library.

title: Sor Juana, the 17th Century Nun Who Became a Mexican (and Feminist) Icon
content:
Long before feminism became a movement, a Catholic nun in colonial Mexico was rewriting the rules of women’s intellectual freedom in the 17th century. Sor (“Sister”) Juana Inés de la Cruz, regarded as the first feminist of the Americas, used her dazzling scholarship, wit and writings to challenge the church’s harsh limitations on women’s right to education.

“One can perfectly well philosophize while cooking supper,” she wrote, ridiculing the idea that women could not engage in serious thought. “You Foolish Men,” she titled a famous satirical poem. Who is more to blame, she mused in verse, “She who sins for pay/or he who pays to sin?” She wrote in both Spanish and in Nahuatl, an Indigenous language, and about both European and Indigenous people, religions and cultures.

This became the stuff of legend.

Celebrated during her lifetime as “The Tenth Muse,” after the nine Muses of Greek mythology, and “The Mexican Phoenix,” after the mythical firebird that rises from its own ashes, she would become an enduring icon of Mexican identity.

title: My Job: Serena Ying-Ting Chiu and the American Folklife Center
content:
-“My Job” is a recurring feature that runs across all Library publications. You can also find this story in the September/October issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

As a library technician at the American Folklife Center, I process archival folklife collections in a wide range of formats — manuscripts, photographs, audio recordings, moving images and digital files — and help make them accessible to researchers and the public. I particularly enjoy the multiformat nature of the work, where I can listen to everything from wax cylinder recordings to reel-to-reel tapes to contemporary digital formats.

My path to AFC was not a direct one. Originally from Taiwan, I came to the United States to study music at the University of Maryland — I’m a classically trained pianist. When I decided to change careers, I started thinking about working in a library. I felt the two fields share something in common: You can discover hidden treasures in both worlds.
